title: The Cost of Maternal Absence
author: Daisy Mae Inglese
summary: Daisy Mae Inglese reviews Erica Komisar's Being There: Why Prioritizing Motherhood in the First Three Years Matters, calling it essential reading for families. She summarizes Komisar's argument that a mother's physical and emotional presence in the first three years shapes a child's physical, emotional and mental development, and that distraction and stress can undermine presence even when a mother is home. The review credits Komisar with overturning the narrative of children as a burden to be handed off and with restoring motherhood as a fulfilling vocation, while also offering practical guidance. Its main criticism is that the book gives too little attention to the economic realities that make three years at home impossible for many families. Inglese widens the lens to ask whether Western economic and cultural priorities have organized family life in ways that put children last.

Komisar argues that a mother’s physical and emotional presence during the first three years of a child’s life plays a fundamental role in their physical, emotional and mental development. But she looks beyond physical presence to what happens when mothers are not emotionally available—when distraction and stress make it harder to respond to their children with patience and attention.

The book begins by dismantling the myths of modern motherhood with developmental psychology and neuroscience, rejecting the assumptions that any caregiver will suffice and that infants should become independent as quickly as possible.

The dominant narrative today casts children as a burden to be managed and handed into the care of others. Komisar not only overturns that narrative but allows another to emerge: motherhood can become one of life’s most fulfilling vocations when women embrace its responsibilities and take that calling seriously.
While it is hard to find fault in this message, the book gives too little attention to the gap between what is ideal for children and the economic realities of contemporary family life.

Once we establish the importance of maternal presence, however, a difficult question follows: what happens when women understand the importance of being at home but lack the economic freedom and social support to make it possible?

To restore the West, we must be willing to ask whether our economic and cultural priorities should bend around the vital needs of children rather than forcing children to adapt to the demands of modern arrangements.
